trigger: You are about to plan a migration of a codebase nobody on the team knows.
body: Write a read-only assessment first (build, runtime, tests, interfaces, deployment, risk list), then have a second, independent reader try to break it before anyone plans from it. Why: even a careful first assessment contained errors and a wrong slice order. Check: every citation in the assessment resolves to a real line, and the second reader's list of missed risks is merged before the plan is frozen.
evidence: A 57 KB assessment of a six-module Java 8 WAR application: 18 of 18 citations resolved and 5 of 5 headline findings held, but with corrections (74 percent of the REST surface sat in 2 of 11 controllers, not 71 percent in 14); the reviewer added 14 missed risks including six hard Java 21 breaks.

trigger: The plan has a separate 'just move to the new JDK' slice before the framework upgrade.
body: Treat the JDK uplift, the framework upgrade and the javax-to-jakarta rename as one coupled step unless a scratch build proves otherwise; make the first slice only 'resolve and compile on the old JDK'. Why: old framework, mocking and coverage libraries do not run on the new JDK, so a JDK-only slice cannot go green. Check: build the old code on the new JDK in a scratch copy and list what fails before accepting a split.
evidence: The proposed first slice (Java 21 only, zero behaviour change) was overturned in the first review: Spring 4.3, Spring Security 4.2, Mockito 1.x, JaCoCo 0.7 and an old grid library all blocked the new JDK, and 71 files imported javax packages.

trigger: You are choosing the target framework and JDK versions.
body: Choose targets from the vendors' published end-of-support dates on the day you decide, and prefer the newest generation still in open-source support that your key dependencies already support. Why: the version the team knew was already out of support and the next one was weeks from the same fate. Check: the proposal names the source of each support date, and the dates are re-checked before the first dependency change.
evidence: The first recommendation (Spring Boot 3.5) had lost open-source support three months earlier; the target moved to Boot 4.1 with Spring Framework 7, Spring Security 7, Jackson 3 and Tomcat 11.

trigger: The framework upgrade brings a new database driver, or someone says 'upgrade the database first, it is safe'.
body: Test the new driver against every server version you run (deployed, middle, newest) in a throwaway project, and run the unchanged old build against the new server with seeded data. Why: driver docs rarely state the minimum server, and the answer sets the order of the whole programme and who must decide. Check: a driver-by-server pass/fail matrix with the driver's own error text, and the old artifact's golden responses and smoke checks passing on the new server.
evidence: A document-database driver pinned by the new framework refused the older server versions that were deployed (a wire-protocol version below the driver's minimum) and passed on a current one; the unchanged old build booted, was seeded and passed 16 golden captures and 5 smoke checks on the current server, so 'server first' was provable.

trigger: The repository ships deployment scripts or inventories that you must not run.
body: Read, never run, the deployment scripts and inventories to learn the versions really deployed, and compare them with what code and tests assume. Why: the deployed container and database were years older than anything developers ran and set hard limits on the target. Check: a table of component, deployed version, source line and the target's minimum, reviewed by the system owner.
evidence: The scripts deployed a servlet container too old to host a Jakarta WAR and a database that had been out of support for years; neither was visible from the build files.

trigger: Tests or startup fail only on some machines or networks.
body: Check every XML schema location in Spring configs against the schema mappings inside the jars; any unmapped URL is fetched over the network at startup. Why: one host-name mismatch made startup depend on a live CDN and made most tests fail behind a filtering proxy. Check: list each location with its mapping, start the context with a dead proxy set, and keep a control cell with the fix reverted that fails for the stated reason.
evidence: About 738 of 843 tests failed with HTTP 403 because one schema URL was fetched with the default Java user agent; 7 URLs in 4 context files, 6 mapped, 1 not; the one-line fix loaded offline and survived a dead proxy.

trigger: Someone labels a red test 'pre-existing'.
body: Do not call a red test pre-existing until a run on the original tree shows the same test red; otherwise call it not yet explained. Why: errors labelled pre-existing were in fact introduced by the migration. Check: the claim cites a run on the old stack with the same test and the same result.
evidence: Ten errors labelled pre-existing had 0 errors on the Java 8 baseline; the cause was that Mockito 1's any(Class) matched null while Mockito 5's does not.

trigger: You cannot port everything and must decide what is in and out of scope.
body: List files and line counts from the old tag, write one inclusion rule for code and templates, define what a stub is and set a cut limit before cutting; record each cut in a ledger the day it happens, and search kept code for imports of every cut part. Why: scope becomes a lookup, not an argument, and a cut that worked is not forgotten. Check: the ledger total is under the limit and no kept module still imports a cut one.
evidence: A Python 2 port of a 2012 web shop cut 482 of 18,313 lines (2.6 percent, limit about 3,660) and 5 of 98 templates; a cut shipping label that had worked was found only via the ledger; in a Django move two of five cut add-ons were still imported by kept code.

trigger: You are about to count tests on old code that has never run on today's machine, or rebuild an old environment from its requirements file.
body: Before counting tests, try to start the old code on the intended interpreter and list every install and import error: pinned libraries that cap the language version, native libraries, and download sources that no longer exist (look for copies on the main package index). Why: a start-up blocker makes every later number meaningless. Check: each failure has a recorded cause, and re-running with the environment fixed shows how many failures flip.
evidence: A 2021 Django 2.2 shop would not run on Python 3.9 only because one enum library pin capped it; all seven source-host links in a 2012 shop's requirements were dead and package-index copies saved the run; a locale variable fixed 14 of 25 failures.

trigger: A tool or plan classifies legacy Python source as Python 2 or 3 by whether it parses.
body: Decide the dialect from definitive markers: Python 2 only from tokens (print statement, <>, backticks, exec statement, L suffix, old octal), Python 3 only from the parse tree; treat except-comma as neutral and give the rule a default when no evidence exists. Why: newer Python 3 accepts 'except X, e:' and tokenizes <> differently by version. Check: parse counts and classification agree on the oldest and newest interpreter over the same corpus.
evidence: Satchmo 0.9.2: 445 of 492 files parse on Python 3.10 but 462 on 3.14; 33 files carry Python 2 markers and none carry Python 3 ones; five files fell back to a partial read on 3.10.

trigger: You list which dependencies block a PHP framework upgrade from Composer's resolver output, or choose the old PHP to run a legacy app.
body: Resolve each direct dependency alone against the target framework and PHP, check pairwise conflicts among the rest, then confirm with one resolve without the confirmed blockers; read the locked packages' PHP bounds before choosing the old runtime, and climb PHP only as far as each framework step needs. Why: the resolver names the first requirement, not the cause, and an old error handler turns new deprecations into fatals. Check: the final resolve without the blockers succeeds.
evidence: Crater on Laravel 13: remove-and-retry named 13 blockers, 8 of them false (the real cause was an old test-runner plugin pin); the lock allowed only PHP 8.0.2 to 8.2 though composer.json said 7.4 or 8.0; the old suite died on PHP 8.4 at a deprecation in an old console package.

trigger: You scope an 'improve it as well' round after a port, or review money code in an old product.
body: Count a fault only if it also exists in the original version, keep a failing test that runs against the old version too, and reproduce every code-read lead as counted, rejected or reproduced-but-design. Why: it separates inherited faults from port regressions and keeps the claim honest. Check: new tests fail on the old version on behaviour, and an independent read confirms the count.
evidence: 20 inherited money faults were found (a refund of 100 returned 89.80 with two tax classes, a cash payment never recorded, two coupons driving a basket below zero, an assert-only currency check that vanishes with python -O) plus 3 caused by the move; one lead was rejected because a docstring says it is intended.

trigger: You plan a move to a newer language version.
body: Probe the new version early: import every pinned package on it, install every pin with binary-only wheels and list the gaps, search your own code for each name in the version's removal and changed-default lists, and record new warning classes (invalid escapes, resource warnings, deprecations) as next-step work. Why: one import-time line in a dependency can stop every test from starting. Check: a per-project list of import failures, missing wheels, watch-list hits and warning classes.
evidence: A payment SDK read a standard-library name removed in Python 3.14 at import, so all 34 test modules of a payout platform failed to load; a 5-line stub restored 491 passed; only 1 of 81 pins lacked a 3.14 wheel.

trigger: Before a migration, or a big step in one, is dispatched as if it were settled.
body: Send an independent reader a blind brief (the outcome wanted, what triggered it, the size; never the pitch) and ask whether the work should be done at all, in this shape, now. Why: the person who proposed it is too close to judge its size, and a wrong-sized migration costs weeks. Check: a recorded verdict (proceed, reshape, probe, stop) and what you did with it; see the agenttalk.challenge skill.
evidence: Two practice tasks (a Python 3.14 probe and a Kubernetes pod-spec study) were reshaped by a challenge verdict before work began; its question 'which environment has nobody run this on?' led to the multi-worker database run that found the overselling.

trigger: You are recording the 'before' result that the migration will be gated on, or a module reports zero or surprisingly few tests.
body: Record, for each module separately, the list of test ids and outcomes (run, failed, error, skipped) on the old stack, and compare the tests discovered with the test methods written in the source. Gate each module on its own id list with the same known failures. Why: a whole-suite total cannot gate one module, and tests the runner never found hide coverage. Check: the discovered count equals the test methods in the source, and the gate names the module and its ids.
evidence: The baseline was 848 tests (2 + 843 + 3 over three modules) and a brief demanded 'backend 848'; one module discovered 0 tests (an include miss) and a test class whose name did not match the runner's pattern hid 3 methods, moving the baseline from 845 to 848.

trigger: The test suite needs a database or other service and 'passes' while that service is down (a vacuous green).
body: Before trusting any green, stop the database or other required service and confirm the suite goes red; remove every catch block in test listeners that swallows connection failures. Why: a suite that is green with its dependency down is a vacuous baseline that will pass any migration. Check: the run with the service down fails with errors, not a smaller green run.
evidence: A listener swallowed database failures; with the database stopped the run showed 15 of 15 errors only after the swallows were removed, and a guard against a non-local database host failed in about 2 seconds with 0 tests run.

trigger: The framework upgrade changes JSON handling, content negotiation, charset or error handling.
body: Before changing anything, capture real responses for every kind of route (body, status, content type, charset) as fixtures with authentication, include one non-ASCII body, and prove the harness catches a renamed field and a pure reorder. Why: no existing test pinned the wire format, so every serialisation or header change would be silent. Check: renaming one field fails exactly one fixture, a reorder fails too, and recording is deterministic on a wiped database.
evidence: 0 of 848 tests pinned JSON shape; 16, then 17, then 44 fixtures were captured; 8 of 15 initially pinned no object and 3 were empty arrays until one row each was seeded; 13 ASCII-only samples hid a charset change.

trigger: The security configuration is hand-built and the target framework's DSL has new defaults.
body: Write one test per security default that could flip (CSRF, headers, session handling, exception translation, request cache, URL firewall), pin today's behaviour on the old stack, prove the real filter chain is installed in the test, and pin the ordered list of filter classes. Why: no test ran the chain, and the new DSL adds filters and defaults silently. Check: without the chain half the pins fail; removing one filter fails exactly one test.
evidence: 0 of 848 tests ran the security chain; 14 pins were written on the old stack and 13 held on the new, one (an encoded slash) flipped and became a decision; a 13-filter chain became 18 on the first DSL port and 15 after the fix.

trigger: Before the first line of a port or framework upgrade is changed, you need a black-box acceptance suite to judge it by.
body: Have someone who has not seen the upgrade write a black-box suite that drives the running app over HTTP, run it on the old version, freeze it outside both code bases and run the same file (same hash) on every step. Change it only through a declared, reviewed new version that states what the old version returns, and rerun that version on the old code and on every earlier step. Why: it settles arguments about done, but a frozen suite can itself be wrong. Check: outcomes are compared per test id between the old version and each step, and every new version has a recorded reason.
evidence: In a Laravel 8 to 13 upgrade 248 own tests stayed green at every step while a 105-test outside suite found two faults they missed (no PDF could be made; reports refused every user); a 4-check suite ran unchanged on a Python 2.7 shop and on its 3.13 port.

trigger: You write or fix an outside-in suite that will be frozen and used to judge an upgrade.
body: Give the frozen suite its own negative controls: match whole labelled values (the right currency or unit), use non-unit rates and distinct non-zero values wherever numbers are summed, read back the record you edited, and prove that the server answering on the port is yours. Why: the yardstick can be wrong where no application break reaches, so a broken app passes. Check: near-miss values (127.50 for 27.50, a wrong currency), a port already taken and a skipped step each turn the suite red.
evidence: Frozen suites for a web shop and an invoicing app: a substring match passed 127.50 for 27.50; every report fixture used exchange rate one so summing raw totals was invisible; a date stored with a time of day dropped the last day of a period.

trigger: You start a port where the old version is ancient or its environment is hard to rebuild.
body: Make the old version run first, pinned, from one script that builds it from nothing: use a prebuilt old runtime instead of compiling one, pin old installers for the before environment only, pin library releases to the old framework, and export old tags without large-file pointers you cannot fetch. Why: asking the running old system beats guessing from code. Check: the script builds the old environment on a clean machine and the old tests run.
evidence: Every behaviour question in a Python 2.7 to 3.13 shop port was answered by the running old shop; its baseline needed Python 2.7.18 unpacked without admin rights, 2010-era C extensions built with relaxed compiler flags and a library pinned to a Django 1.3 release; a Laravel 8 baseline needed a pinned older PHP.

trigger: Old tests fail before you have changed anything, or you are about to freeze a baseline.
body: Run the old suite first, from a fresh clone, record every failing test id with a written cause, and compare ids, not totals, on every later run. Why: otherwise inherited failures get blamed on the upgrade, or a test-data problem gets 'fixed' as a bug. Check: a stored id-and-outcome list for the old version, with every red test carrying a cause.
evidence: Shuup (Django 2.2 to 5.2): 1,318 passed, 10 skipped and 0 failed on the same test ids before and after the first step; the Windows runs showed 9 set-up failures that passed on Linux. Satchmo: 5 wrong-total payment tests failed because a data file referred to two optional parts the demo leaves out.

trigger: Tests fail at some times of day (for example around midnight or month end) or only in the full suite.
body: Suspect fixed historical dates against now-relative data, or a UTC date compared with a local date, before suspecting the code; anchor fixtures to the test's own day and freeze the clock. Why: the failure looks like time-of-day but is a drifted fixture, and it wastes review rounds. Check: the test passes in isolation under three time zones, and the frozen suite passes at month end and between 00:00 and 02:00 local time.
evidence: 25 failures in a Java suite were a fixed 2016 date against a record attached to 'now minus 5 years'; an original time-based test failed only between 00:00 and 02:00 local time; period-end reports went red when a fiscal period rolled over.

trigger: Development happens on Windows with git autocrlf and fixtures, hashes or shell scripts cross to Linux.
body: Set autocrlf off before creating worktrees, commit fixtures and shell scripts with LF (text eol=lf), count CR bytes in Python rather than grep, write files back in binary mode, and run recipes once from a fresh clone on the target platform. Why: line endings changed fixtures, hashes and scripts between Windows and Linux and buried real edits in whole-file diffs. Check: zero CR bytes per commit except named files, git diff --stat shows only intended lines, and the recipe passes on Linux twice.
evidence: A '17 of 17 green' recorded on a CRLF working copy was really 15 red; a 143-line diff held 24 real changes; a Windows-committed shell script failed on its first line on Linux.

trigger: A black-box suite or probe runs against a local server or a scratch checkout, and a result looks surprisingly good or bad.
body: Prove which code and which server produced the result: print the imported module's file path (isolated mode ignores PYTHONPATH and a worktree has no editable install), call the interpreter by full path, use a fresh port and confirm the listener is yours in its own log. Why: suites passed against another server on the same port or tested the installed copy. Check: the printed path is inside the checkout and the server log shows every request.
evidence: Three times a black-box suite hit another server on the same port and passed; a probe looked like a mass regression only because the installed package was imported; a launcher shim ran a Python without the test plugin.

trigger: You hand over or integrate a test harness that must run on two toolchains (old and ported language, runner or client library).
body: Before the first comparison, run the harness's own self-tests and one capture on the old and the new toolchain, make it read the summary format of each test-tool version, and treat any port-only red as a harness bug to fix with a failing test first. Why: a harness checked only on the old side hides faults that appear only on the port. Check: self-tests and a capture are green on both sides and captures hold no memory addresses or other per-run noise.
evidence: A fault runner written for pytest 2.8 would have marked every pytest 5 run invalid; self-tests failed on a temp folder on another drive; a recorder logged an object with a memory address so differences changed every run.

trigger: You execute a multi-step uplift, or a gate passes on one machine and fails on another.
body: Make one commit per planned step, run the gate as one command from a clean tree and clean build output with no continue-on-failure switch, quote the outcome (first test classes run, counts), not the flag you passed, and write down where you are before any run longer than ten minutes. Why: uncommitted work died with sessions, a warm build directory hid an incomplete port, and a hard-coded order made 'reverse order' gates alphabetical. Check: each step has a commit id, a gate log from deleted output and a recorded count.
evidence: A module 'passed' but failed from clean because one file still imported the old Jackson package; eleven 'both orders' gates were all alphabetical and a real reverse run showed a 371-error cascade; after a host reboot only committed work survived.

trigger: You plan a multi-version framework upgrade.
body: Move one framework major version per step with the same test selection, a tag and a recorded result per step, and finish with a language-version-only step (climb the language only as far as each framework step needs). Why: failures group by cause and trace to one change, and the dangerous changes raise no error. Check: each step has a tag and a re-runnable table of tests, warnings and advisories.
evidence: Django 2.2 to 3.2 to 4.2 to 5.2: failures fell 108, 22, 11, 10 at the first step and 581, 484, 96, 17, 10 at the second; Laravel 8 to 13 used six tagged steps plus a PHP-8.5-only step; known advisories fell 208, 169, 52.

trigger: A framework step turns a green run into hundreds of red tests.
body: Group failures by error line (sort and count) before opening any test, fix the biggest group first in one place, rerun only failing files, then do one full run. Why: hundreds of failures usually come from a handful of causes. Check: a table maps each group to one fix and the count of distinct error lines falls after each fix.
evidence: Django 2.2 to 3.2: 108 failures came from about 8 causes; the next jump's 581 failures came from about 10 and ended at 10 remaining.

trigger: The code compiles after moving a library to a new major version, or the old parent pom pins versions the new BOM also manages.
body: Read the resolved dependency tree: if the old major is still on the classpath transitively, the port can be half done and still compile; audit every version-management entry against the effective POM and drop old pins the BOM manages. Why: compile success proved nothing, and old pins over the BOM broke the first real boot. Check: the tree shows no old-major artifacts, a grep for old package names is zero, and the built archive's jar list is compared before and after.
evidence: 20 main files still used Jackson 2 yet modules compiled because the new library pulled 2.21 in; pinned logback 1.2.3 and SLF4J 1.7 over the BOM broke the first boot; a 'commons-collections' override had the wrong artifact id and never applied.

trigger: A serialisation library changes major version, or JSON output differs after the upgrade though the fields are the same.
body: Dump every feature default from old and new, list the flips and new enforcements, restore the old values in one shared factory for read as well as write, sweep for bare constructions, and compare field order per domain class against the old jar. Why: goldens cover only the write side; read-side flips accept malformed input and a changed ordering rule reorders output. Check: an effective-value probe on the built mapper and tests that fail first, before the fix.
evidence: A census (93 old, 141 new features) found 11 flips and 3 new enforcements; 4 write-side defaults showed in goldens, the 11 read-side flips only in a cold read (unknown properties accepted, messages with a null timestamp dropped); a constructor-ordering default reordered 9 of 62 classes; six bare mapper sites changed login response order.

trigger: You upgrade from an old mocking library to a current major version.
body: Port matchers by their old semantics (Mockito 1's any(Class) matched null), treat each changed call site as a finding, and expect XML-configured mocks to pick new overloads. Why: the old matcher quietly let production code pass null and the new one fails. Check: a failing-first count (10 of 13 red) then all green after switching to nullable or any, each site named.
evidence: Matchers became ArgumentMatchers in 11 files with about 50 retyped; Spring XML picked a new reified overload and needed a wrapper; a verifyZeroInteractions rename was first introduced wrongly.

trigger: Tests pass or fail depending on class order or machine.
body: Look for JVM-static holders (application context, registries) that every context refreshes so the last writer wins; reset them in base classes and add a probe that fails with the reset disabled. Why: order-dependent suites look like random flakes and are not reproducible across machines. Check: reverse-order and random-seed runs give identical counts, and the probe fails with the reset removed.
evidence: Adding one new test class changed filesystem order and reddened 25 tests; a static registry stayed empty until production-context tests refreshed it, giving 19 order-only errors; tests that cleared system properties instead of restoring them produced a 371-error cascade.

trigger: The new stack is stricter about paths (trailing slash, encoded slash, double slash).
body: Probe trailing slash, encoded slash and double slash on both stacks, including the old container deployed locally, and grep the frontend for emitters before accepting a flip. Why: router, firewall and connector each now reject URLs the old stack served. Check: a table of probe, old result, new result and layer; every accepted flip is pinned.
evidence: Trailing-slash matching was removed (every route 200 to 404, 0 frontend emitters); %2F in a search path was rejected by the firewall; 6 dialogs sent a double slash the old container tolerated and the new connector rejected, so the frontend was fixed and a smoke assertion added.

trigger: A config profile, deployment template or schedule expression has never been parsed by the application.
body: Write a parse test for every profile and deployment template, assert the next fire times of schedule expressions, and do not fix an expression to what you think it meant: compare with the other profiles. Why: a malformed cron sat inert in one profile and a first fix changed the schedule. Check: a test over tracked profiles with a drift guard on the profile list, and two next fire times asserted.
evidence: A 7-field cron the new scheduler rejects sat in a profile; the first repair (daily at 1 AM) was wrong and the right one (monthly) matched every other profile; 13 expressions and 6 deployment templates were later parsed.

trigger: You replace Python 2 StringIO, cStringIO or md5-of-text code during a port.
body: Decide per call site whether data is text or binary: archive and image buffers need BytesIO, hashes need an explicit encoding that reproduces old values, and decoding adds UnicodeDecodeError that a read-error-only handler misses. Why: a blind swap imports cleanly and fails only when the archive is built or read. Check: an export and re-import round trip with real bytes, the same hash-derived folder names on both versions, and invalid UTF-8 input.
evidence: Replacing cStringIO with io.StringIO broke ZIP export and import in a 2012 shop; an md5 over a username changed type and the fix kept folder names like 6/3/alice; a marker reader crashed on invalid UTF-8 and could overwrite a pass record.

trigger: Code sorts or lists by a key that can tie, or old output depended on dict or set order.
body: Give every sort or listing whose key can tie an explicit key function with a defined tie-break, and decide in writing what was arbitrary in the old output. Why: Python 2 compared anything and kept an arbitrary order; Python 3 raises TypeError or follows insertion order. Check: feed tied inputs to every sorted listing and compare old against new.
evidence: Two options with the same sort order fell through to comparing model objects and raised TypeError; in a ranking even the old stack returned amy,bob,cat in one run and cat,bob,amy in another; 3 of 6 blind runs never saw the tie order.

trigger: You move a Django project with its own AppConfig classes to Django 4.1 or newer.
body: Dump every installed app's configuration class (name, label, class path) before and after each step and compare; set default=True on the class and keep the apps module importable. Why: Django 4.1 silently ignores the old default-app-config setting, so apps lose menus, providers and signals with no error. Check: the dump is identical before and after and a fresh migrate works.
evidence: In a Shuup 2.2 to 5.2 move a dump of all 41 apps per step compared equal and all 296 models kept their table names.

trigger: You move to Django 5 a project that keeps model objects in sessions or filters by new unsaved objects.
body: Grep forms, views and templates for filters on an unsaved instance and related-manager calls that can run on a new object, and guard them with a pk check. Keep primary keys in the session rather than model objects; if you keep a serializer that rebuilds objects, let it name only installed models and round-trip literal marker values as values. Why: Django 2.2 quietly returned nothing, 5 raises, and checkout kept unsaved objects in sessions. Check: open every create page in a test client and round-trip an unsaved object and a decimal.
evidence: Coupon and campaign creation forms failed on Django 5; a later independent read found session data that was a literal marker coming back as an object.

trigger: A port 'imports cleanly' and you consider the layer done.
body: Load real fixtures and exercise save, str and admin of every model, visit each view, and sweep by class of removed API and Python 3 change (render with a dict not Context, add on unsaved objects, empty mail recipients). Why: removed APIs called inside functions fail only when the line runs. Check: fixture load and a save of every model succeed, and the last step of every flow (the mail, the first add to cart) is tested.
evidence: A package init calling a removed get_apps() passed import and check on 97 modules and failed on the first Product.save; a runtime sweep of every model and admin page found 10 bugs import checks missed; the order mail failed with 'context must be a dict'.

trigger: After any library or framework upgrade that runs the app's own database migrations, even with no code change.
body: Build a fresh database from the real migrations on the old and new commit, dump columns (type, nullable, default), indexes and foreign keys per table, and treat every difference beyond the intended ones as a finding; run makemigrations --check twice and do not wrap lists of allowed values in a function, which makes the generator report changes every time. Why: libraries change schemas themselves, so new installs differ from existing ones. Check: the diff holds only declared differences.
evidence: Between Django 4.2 and 5.2, 35 tables differed (33 translation tables, 2 file-manager tables); in Laravel 11 a column change made one new-install column NOT NULL (1 of 14 calls) and SQLite foreign key drops failed 7 migrations; a choices wrapper made makemigrations report changes on every run.

trigger: You move a project that stores money, quantity or measurement decimals to Django 5.
body: Round money, quantity and measurement decimals to the field's decimal places in your own code before saving, and check boundary ties with the original input on both versions, including exact and range lookups. Why: Django 5 no longer rounds a decimal to the field's places before handing it to the database, and a fix in a general preparation hook also rounds query operands. Check: a boundary-tie test passes on old and new and the same lookups return the same rows.
evidence: A price example that was an exact tie on SQLite passed on Django 2.2 and failed on 5.2 (SQLite kept a double and read it back rounded the other way); plain decimal fields such as percentages keep the unrounded behaviour, recorded as accepted.

trigger: You upgrade a library that carries locale data (Babel, CLDR) and the app parses typed amounts.
body: Feed old user-entered amount formats for each supported locale through the real form handler and declare any accepted-behaviour change. Why: new data can change separator characters, so a typed amount that was accepted is refused. Check: a table of old formatted amounts per locale shows accept or reject on the new stack.
evidence: Babel moved the French grouping space from U+00A0 to U+202F, so '1 000,00' typed the old way got HTTP 400 with no tip saved; only fr and fr_fr of 33 languages changed (671 comparisons).

trigger: A date library moves from lenient to strict typing (Carbon 2 to 3) in an app that stores settings as text.
body: Search unit calls whose argument is a variable and convert settings stored as text to whole numbers at each use the way the old library did ('7' is 7, '7.5' is 7, empty is 0), checking whether a real null can reach the call. Why: the new library throws TypeError for text the old one accepted, mostly in paths tests never reach. Check: test text, empty, non-numeric and null values at each call site against the old version.
evidence: Seven places failed in Crater (fiscal-year start, estimate conversion, invoice copy, recurring due date, link expiry); four own tests failed and three of the seven had no test; a real null added 1 unit in Carbon 2 and adds 0 in 3.

trigger: A framework step moves any package across a major version.
body: For each package that crosses a major version, read its upgrade notes, diff your published config against the package default two levels deep, name every key it reads with the old value, check every imported class still exists and run the real code path. Why: renames, new columns and nested keys surface only when the path runs, and defaults merge only one level deep. Check: a written note per package and a test per fault that fails without the fix.
evidence: Across five package majors in a Laravel upgrade, uploads failed (new column), every backup notice failed (renamed classes), boot failed (a missing nested key), a queued job broke (removed factory method) and a PDF facade moved, one of them surfacing only five steps later.

trigger: A mail, proxy, TLS, cookie or permission library crosses a major version while you keep the old security configuration.
body: Compare behaviour, not the setting value, with scripted input on the real transport: a server without STARTTLS must receive no credentials, a visitor-supplied forwarded address must not change the client address, and unscoped permission checks must still behave. Why: a key can load fine while the new library ignores it or changes its meaning. Check: each refusal is probed on old and new and diffed.
evidence: After Laravel 9 the mail 'TLS' choice was ignored so logins could go out in clear text; at Laravel 13 trust-all-proxies let a visitor pick their client address and get a fresh rate limit per reset request; after a permissions library 1.0, report pages refused the owner.

trigger: Your tests only check that a background job was queued, or an upgrade touches a package that stores or lists artifacts.
body: For every job class the app dispatches add a test that runs the job for real on throwaway inputs and checks its output, seed one real stored artifact for list and download paths, run both on the old commit and on every step, and grep for fake( to find unrun jobs. Why: a faked queue proves a job was queued, never that it can run, and empty-list tests pass after a method is removed. Check: green on the old commit, red on a step that removes an API the job uses.
evidence: Crater's tests only checked that a backup was queued; every backup died on an undefined constant when the process-control extension is missing, and a removed factory method broke job building, hidden for four steps; both management pages called a removed size method.

trigger: You upgrade an embedded infrastructure library, or run test suites on a machine that may reach the internet.
body: Run the test and smoke suites behind an egress block or a recording proxy, and switch off every library's phone-home and cloud-metadata probing in production config. Why: default usage reporting sent hundreds of outbound requests per test run before anyone looked. Check: a count of outbound attempts per run, and zero with the switch set.
evidence: An embedded clustering library made 8 cloud-metadata requests and 1 HTTPS connect per member per test (32 and 4 in one new test); one environment flag brought both to 0.

trigger: The first full build on the new JDK or language version goes red before any of your own code is touched.
body: Pull build-plugin, coverage and mock-library upgrades forward as the new runtime demands them, and give legacy libraries temporary open-up flags only with an end date. Why: the old test-runner plugin crashed on the new runtime and old reflection libraries needed flags, so the build was red for reasons unrelated to your code. Check: each temporary flag has a removal commit and the final build uses none.
evidence: In a Java 8 to 21 move the old surefire plugin threw a NullPointerException on JDK 21, an old data library needed --add-opens until it was ported, and a parameter-name library needed -parameters.

trigger: Your gates all assemble contexts in-process, or you move from an external application server to an embedded one.
body: Deploy the actual built archive on the target container with a real database and drive it with a browser (render, failed login, successful login, authenticated read, a mutation check that fails when a field is renamed). Why: every in-process gate was green while the shipped archive could not boot, route or log in. Check: the smoke runs as a standing gate with the archive's jar count and a hash that changes when the build changes.
evidence: The first real boot failed on a logging jar pin, the second on a circular reference, the third had no dispatcher servlet; a fourth login failure was a seed erased by test cleanup.

trigger: You add a pin, guard, golden or any new check to a suite.
body: Show each new test red against a deliberately broken version of what it protects (mutation) and red against the old code (failing-first), and state what it does not pin; run the clean suite first and count a mutant caught only when the intended test was collected, ran and failed on its assertion (an import error or a smaller green run is not a catch). Why: many pins stayed green with the mechanism removed. Check: two quoted outcomes per test; a mutation that stays green is a finding.
evidence: Two named-mechanism cells stayed green with the mechanism removed; four green point pins looked like a surface until an 8-case table replaced them; a missing plugin made every mutant look killed on one interpreter.

trigger: You claim 'does not connect out', 'is offline' or 'was rejected'.
body: Run a control: the same test with the fix reverted must show the failure, and an owned stand-in host outside the environment must be unreachable (never aim probes at a live service). Why: an absence of failure may mean the path was never exercised. Check: a 2x2 matrix (fix and proxy flags) in which the control cell fails for the stated reason, with a computed verdict of blocked, reached or inconclusive.
evidence: With the schema fix reverted and a dead proxy the control gave ConnectException rather than HTTP 403, proving the flags were live; a probe through a directly served file showed the proxy while real routed requests bypassed it.

trigger: A recipe builds, deploys and tests, or a comparison reads an output file written by a separate test run.
body: Check the build exit code, hash the artifact and require its timestamp after the build start; bind every run to the code under test with a receipt (run id, exit status, test counts) and delete old output first. Why: a failed build deployed a stale archive that reported green, and a failed run left the last good capture so the comparison passed. Check: distinct commits give distinct hashes, and a planted import error with the same output path makes the comparison fail.
evidence: A 'full green' at a new commit had a byte-identical archive to the previous one because a mangled build argument failed the build and the script ignored the exit code; after a good run an import error left the old capture and the comparison exited 0.

trigger: You prepare the acceptance of the migration.
body: Run the original and the migrated application side by side on the same restored original data and walk every screen and dynamic check, including the old container locally for behaviour the old stack tolerated; keep a tracked acceptance record with a stack table, per-screen results and defects with severities. Why: identical only means something against a measured original. Check: the record exists and every deviation is declared.
evidence: The original dataset restored with zero index rejections and no restart; every screen identical; two deliberate deviations recorded; the locally provisioned old container proved a double-slash tolerance.

trigger: The migration or its test run must not contact external hosts.
body: Enforce no-egress with an OS or firewall rule bound to the exact program paths, or an internal network with no route out, and prove it with a probe that checks isolation first (outside blocked, internal control connects); do not rely on proxy variables. Why: cooperative proxies have many escapes and some HTTP clients ignore proxy variables inside web servers. Check: each toolchain binary fails to reach an owned outside canary host at the socket.
evidence: A string-prefix origin check was passed by a URL with a userinfo section; a newer HTTP client ignored proxy settings in a web server so a tripwire saw nothing for several steps; the firewall block (48 rules for 24 binaries) followed several incidents.

trigger: The team wants a final, tool-based acceptance of the migrated code.
body: Pin an independent toolset with versions and hashes (static analysis, bug patterns, coverage, mutation testing, dependency and removed-API scans, architecture rules, contract tests), record baselines per category and make them fail-closed ratchets. Why: tool output is evidence that does not depend on the team's own tests. Check: a preflight verifies the pins, each ratchet has a negative control, and a full run from a clean checkout is made at the final commit.
evidence: Ten verification profiles went green at the close tip of a Java 21 migration; the tools themselves needed fixes (a culture-dependent parse, an assertion that passed without a run, a bytecode-support pin).

trigger: You build a comparison or differential harness as your evidence.
body: Break a module on purpose and prove the harness goes red; make it fail on import errors, empty case lists, repeated names, unused declarations, missing captures and any network attempt, and compare raw bytes, not decoded text. Why: 'zero different' may mean both sides skipped the same thing. Check: a broken import, an emptied case list and a wildcard declaration each turn the verdict red.
evidence: A harness said '83 same, 0 different' with a payment module's import broken because both sides skipped the same views; it accepted two empty case lists, compared decoded text so byte FF looked like FE, and pinned today's date in three expectations.

trigger: You port code that talks to an outside service (payments, banks) and compare old against new.
body: Capture what is SENT below the HTTP library, compare raw bytes first, let the stand-in record every request field, and allow differences only as one declaration (a written note saying which difference is expected and why) per case and field, with exact values; no wildcards, and unused declarations fail. Why: internal balances can be right while the outgoing request is wrong. Check: doubling an outgoing amount turns a test red and removing a real difference's declaration fails the run.
evidence: A harness for four payment modules: 83 cases (10 same, 17 same apart from order, 56 declared, 0 different, 0 stale, 0 socket attempts) exposed a card authorised twice per capture and payments accepted to another account, currency or amount; a reviewer's doubled payout passed 35 harness tests.

trigger: An acceptance check says 'the success page appeared'.
body: Assert the saved effect (amount stored, row written, stock changed) with non-zero distinct values, call hooks through the real production entry point, and prove each new check with a deliberately broken build that the old suite still passes. Why: a page can say success while nothing was recorded, and hand-made arguments can bypass the production branch. Check: skipping the payment step turns the new check red while the old suite stays green.
evidence: A frozen suite passed with a payment of 0.00 because it checked the success page; two added checks caught it, proved on a broken shop; a cash processor compared its argument with a string while the shop passed an object, so cash orders stayed unpaid for years.

trigger: You count 'N fixes, each with a test'.
body: Remove each fix in a throwaway copy and rerun its test; count it proved only if the intended test was collected, ran, and failed on its assertion without the fix and passes with it. Why: removing a fix can also remove a name the test imports, so a tool that accepts any non-zero exit counts a test that never ran as red. Check: the log shows the test id FAILED with an assertion message; a misspelt name or import error reads NOT PROVED.
evidence: A first tool accepted any failure and counted a test that never ran; the hardened tool covered 23 checks; all 14 fixes of one stage and 22 of 22 in a payout port were proved by removal, and some claims proved larger than their proof.

trigger: You rely on statement coverage as confidence for money code.
body: Plant one-line faults one at a time in the money code (answer applied twice, wrong refund sign, payout at gross amount), count a catch only from a healthy run with a new failing test, include controls (a comment-only change is not caught, a broken file is invalid), and list unreached safeguards. Why: coverage counts lines run, not lines checked. Check: a fault runner restores the file and reports which check caught each fault.
evidence: A suite ran 93 percent of 1,008 money statements yet missed 3 of 14 planted faults; a reviewer's doubled payout passed because ledger balances were right and the matcher ignored the request body; 21 scripted stories caught all 14.

trigger: You port a money engine and must show old and new behave the same.
body: Run scripted stories through the product's own code on old and new, compare the stored tables cell by cell with every difference declared, and show unchanged money code as a byte-for-byte file comparison. Why: it finds differences tests do not ask about without trusting the port's own tests. Check: the diff exits clean except for declared cells, and the money module's hash or diff against the old tag is empty.
evidence: Liberapay: 21 money stories from card payment to lost chargeback; 6 cells differed, all one note (an exception text lost its trailing comma since Python 3.7); PostgreSQL 17 and 9.6 pictures were byte-identical and the money code did not change by one line.

trigger: You plan the verification of a framework upgrade.
body: Use three kinds of checks because each finds different faults: the builder's own extra checks, a pre-written outside-in suite, and an independent read of the code against upgrade notes and what each setting promises. Why: a suite sees what users see, a read sees what a setting promises, and neither alone is enough. Check: each recorded fault is tagged with the check that found it.
evidence: A Laravel 8 to 13 upgrade had 11 faults that 248 own tests missed: reading upgrade notes found 3, running a job for real 1, a schema comparison 1, the outside suite 2, and the code read 3 (TLS mail setting, existing backups, client-address trust).

trigger: You claim a framework step is green, and the evidence is a pass count or totals.
body: Accept a step as green only with the same test ids and the same outcomes, nothing skipped or deleted, built from one process that discovers every test module, and explain any change in assertion count per test. Why: totals hide swapped, skipped or removed tests, and a hand-kept module list undercounts. Check: diff the id-and-outcome lists before and after; the discovered module count equals the report.
evidence: A Django 2.2 to 3.2 step kept 1,318 passed and 10 skipped on the same ids; a report said 262 tests in 31 modules while 49 modules load (308 tests); assertions fell from 657 to 484 because 173 tests each lost one in a counting change, with no check lost.

trigger: A test fails after an upgrade and someone edits its input or expectation to make it pass.
body: Treat a test that fails after an upgrade as a finding: restore the original input, run it on old and new with values printed at each step, name the changed behaviour, and keep a declared list of every edited test with its reason and no new skips (every existing skip explained). Why: nudging an input keeps ids and totals and deletes the case that caught the change. Check: the original input is in the final test and passes on both versions.
evidence: A price test input nudged past a rounding boundary passed; with the original input it passed on Django 2.2 and failed on 5.2 because Django 5 no longer rounds a decimal before storing; in a Laravel upgrade 17 of 248 tests were edited, each for an interface rename, with no expected value changed.

trigger: A port's happy-path journeys and checkout tests all pass.
body: Submit missing and invalid input to every form and endpoint and compare status, body and content type with the old version. Why: a removed error-construction API survives in validation branches that successful journeys never reach. Check: one invalid-input test per form asserting a normal form error, not a server exception.
evidence: A removed forms.util import on an invalid payment choice gave a 500 instead of a form error while every successful checkout passed; a renamed response-helper argument changed error responses and was caught only by posting a bad file to both versions.

trigger: You restore old behaviour after an upgrade (rounding, timezone attach, decoding) with a wrapper or replacement function.
body: Write the test to state what the OLD version returns for edge cases and run it on both versions; list every route to the behaviour (writes, lookups, nested data, both daylight-saving transitions) and avoid helpers whose error cases differ from the original call. Why: a fix for the failing case often changes a neighbouring contract. Check: the same test passes old and new, with a neighbour probe per route.
evidence: In one Django upgrade a restored behaviour broke something three times: rounding applied to lookups changed matches, a time helper raised in the repeated daylight-saving hour, and a restricted decoder left the nested JSON route open.

trigger: You write or grade a differential probe of old against new.
body: Choose inputs by asking what the old stack would have refused, rounded differently or ordered arbitrarily: exact halves (Python 3 round() is half-to-even), tied sort keys, '1_6' and '32.0' in integer fields, ids after deletes; report which inputs ran, not which endpoints. Why: a probe over every endpoint misses changes when no input sits where the versions differ. Check: the report lists edge inputs per type and each ran on both stacks.
evidence: In a blind port of a Django avatar app with six traps, scores ran 3 to 5.5 of 6; only 1 of 6 runs caught that int parsing accepted '1_6'; 2 of 6 never touched rounding; a grid found 41 of 1,620 cells differing.

trigger: A suite is green but uses skips, expected failures or history-dependent tests, or you add an earlier admission check in front of failure-path tests.
body: Read the skip reasons (-rs) of every CI leg, run xfailed defect tests with --runxfail on old and new and diff the failing assertion lines, assert the intended handler was reached, and keep history-dependent tests from skipping. Why: a skip or xfail absorbs any failure, so a new error on the same path or a missing git history hides lost coverage. Check: identical assertion values old and new, and no unexplained SKIPPED.
evidence: 55 downgrade-fence tests skipped on every CI leg because the export had no git history; a report defect stayed xfailed on four steps only because the page was refused with 403; a disconnect test started testing a 403 after a Host header change.

trigger: An upgrade changes which object the framework hands to your code by default (for example the default timezone implementation).
body: For each changed dependency ask which object the normal runtime path supplies, and add a test through that path (the real middleware, the default timezone) rather than one that builds its own legacy object; confirm it fails without the fix and check what mechanical renames touched. Why: tests that activate the legacy object stay green while real requests get the new type. Check: a request-level test fails if a legacy-only call is used on the new default.
evidence: Django 4 uses zoneinfo by default; old localize() calls broke day-and-hour campaigns on the normal path while 581-test runs and tests using pytz directly stayed green; a rename script turned a compatibility alias into a self-assignment.

trigger: The old framework loaded data automatically that the new one does not, and you claim the new schema or database equals the old.
body: Compare the new database to the old table by table and row by row from an empty start with the same fixed data, including data the old framework loaded implicitly (initial_data fixtures before Django 1.9), and recreate it in a migration. Why: structure can match while rows quietly go missing. Check: row counts per table match and a saved per-table comparison is built at the final commit.
evidence: Django 1.3 loaded initial_data fixtures automatically and Django 5 does not; a 'tables match' claim missed 13 contact-role rows, 2 tax classes and 2 image rows in a ported 2012 shop.

trigger: One risk is covered by several layered protections (for example a lock, a unique index and a check in code).
body: Test each layer alone as well as removing it: take the other layers away and see whether the layer under test still stops the fault. Why: removing one of several layers may change nothing, so a removal proof can pass while that layer is untested. Check: for each layer, a test that disables all the other layers and goes red when that layer is removed.
evidence: A practice port onto a key-value store and a queue, run against local stand-ins: removing one of several protections changed nothing (one run).

trigger: You audit licences, install scripts or advisories of a JavaScript module that the migration builds.
body: Audit the lockfile, not the installed folder, and fail when the lockfile has no package map or the audit scanned zero packages. Why: the installed tree holds only the packages for your own operating system, and an old lockfile format passed with zero packages scanned. Check: a fixture lockfile in the old format makes the audit exit non-zero, and the scanned count equals the lockfile's.
evidence: An audit covered 62 installed packages while the lockfile listed 109, including 47 platform binaries.

trigger: The old front end builds with a toolchain from years ago and its built output is part of the contract.
body: Pin the Node and npm versions inside the project, fingerprint the built output as a tree hash, and prove it with two clean builds and one build on a different Node version; keep the old libraries unchanged if byte-identical output is the contract. Why: a global Node version rewrote the lockfile and an unmaintained headless browser hung the test phase. Check: the same fingerprint on three machines, and a build without the pin fails loudly.
evidence: A 356-file output fingerprint reproduced six times; a global Node 24 rewrote a lockfile by 4,190 added and 1,965 removed lines.

trigger: A change touches stock, orders or any check-then-write, or you move from a single dev server to several workers.
body: Run concurrency probes on the production-grade database with several web workers and judge saved effects (stock, orders, payments), not HTTP statuses; also try cold workers with overlapping first requests and share per-process caches across workers. Why: single-threaded or SQLite runs hide races, half-imported modules and caches that lose state between steps. Check: the record names database, worker count and repeated runs, and the pass condition is read from the database.
evidence: On PostgreSQL with 4 gunicorn workers, 12 shoppers for 5 items oversold in every run of the improved shop while a laptop SQLite run said pass; a per-process cache lost the card between checkout steps in 24 to 25 of 48 checkouts; a cold worker failed 2 of about 40 overlap runs.

trigger: You make a multi-step write all-or-nothing in one transaction around a check-then-change on shared counts.
body: Lock the shared rows first in a fixed key order and check inside the lock, and run the old version through the same probe as a baseline. Why: a transaction hides writes until commit, so a gap of milliseconds between check and decrease becomes the length of the whole operation. Check: a concurrent probe on PostgreSQL shows stock never negative and sold never above supply, with old and new results in one record.
evidence: The original shop never oversold (6 of 6 runs); after one transaction per order it oversold every run (7 or 8 sold of 5, stock -2 or -3); after locking stock rows in product-id order, 24 shoppers sold exactly 5 in 21 of 21 runs.

trigger: You add a once-per-order guard (capture, authorise, notify) behind a row lock.
body: Decide from values read under the lock (locked order, balance, paid flag, pending row) and compute amounts inside it, never from values the caller worked out before the lock. Why: a second request that read the balance before the first committed recorded a second authorisation or an overpayment. Check: a deterministic test where request B reads the balance, A completes, then B continues, red on the old code.
evidence: Two double-authorisation fixes were rejected for skipping the guard when an amount was passed (balance ended at -120); a cash remainder computed before the lock recorded 110 on a 100 order (80 owed plus a 10 deposit).

trigger: You test a checkout or payment step for concurrency, including a double-submit of one order.
body: Test two ways: many different shoppers, and one shopper confirming ONE order several times at once, in every payment mode (capture, authorise then capture, void, callback). Why: the first never shows duplicate completion of the same order, and a guard in one mode does not protect the others. Check: counts of sold, stock, discount uses and payment rows match the number of orders in each mode.
evidence: A 20-shopper probe passed while 20 shoppers each confirming one order four times at once gave 20 to 26 problems per run (sold up to 4x, negative stock, 80 discount uses for 20 orders); with capture-later on, two authorisations still counted the sale twice.

trigger: You write a test for an 'at the same moment' claim (no double spend, no double count).
body: Use two real database connections (threads) on the production-grade database, hold the first inside the race window with an event, and prove the test by removing the fix and watching it fail on a count (for example the fake provider's call count). Why: SQLite's write lock serialises races away and nested calls on one connection prove nothing. Check: with the guard removed the test fails every time; with it, it passes every time.
evidence: Race tests for a charge-once guard on PostgreSQL: 10 of 10 pass; guard removed, 10 of 10 fail with 2 provider calls instead of 1; the first three such tests in a payments port passed with the lock removed and were rejected.

trigger: You report a clean concurrency run or a 'zero database errors' result, which is easy to overclaim.
body: Call a clean concurrency run evidence, not proof: name the machine, database version, workers, run counts per scenario and the scenarios not probed, and run a zero-errors log search on a previous round's log that has known errors. Why: a race that did not happen in one run says nothing about the next, and a search that never finds anything proves nothing. Check: the report lists scenarios, run counts and untested ones.
evidence: A payment race failed in 1 of 6 runs in the original and 1 of 6 in an earlier fixed state, with a window of a few milliseconds; fixed, 0 of 21; the zero-errors claim was checked against the previous round's log, which gave 21.

trigger: Code calls an external provider to take money and then saves locally.
body: Before the call, commit a 'charge in flight' claim under the order lock; sort every provider answer into charged, declined-and-safe-to-retry or unknown, let only the middle group retry, and let only staff clear unknown. Why: a local rollback never undoes an external charge, so you need claims, idempotency keys and reconciliation. Check: with the claim removed the same-moment test sees 2 provider calls, and failing the local save after approval refuses the retry.
evidence: Two simultaneous confirmations both charged the provider; a retry after 'approved, local save failed' charged twice with one record; with the claim, 10 of 10 race runs passed and 10 of 10 failed without it.

trigger: You map a payment provider's response codes to a 'declined' outcome.
body: Make unknown the default, check each retry-safe code against the provider's public code table, and treat held or review answers as unknown. Why: a held charge can still be approved later, so booking it as declined lets the shopper pay twice. Check: undoing the classification fails the classification tests, and each declined code links to a table row and states what must change before a retry.
evidence: One gateway's 'held for review' code was booked as declined and caused two charges; a table sorting each code three ways made 25 classification checks fail when undone; recurring billing still treated unrecognised results as declines.

trigger: A payment touches an order plus a second balance (voucher, stock), or you fix a payment race in one payment method.
body: Lock every balance that governs a transfer in one fixed order and re-read before computing, reserve the amount against every other payment method while a claim is open, and give each lock its own test that fails without it. Why: locking only one side lets two sources pay one order, and sibling methods stay free to pay the same order. Check: two vouchers on one order end with one payment, and a card claim blocks a voucher.
evidence: On PostgreSQL two different gift certificates could both pay one order until the order was locked first; while a card claim was out a gift certificate could still pay the full order; opposite lock order between two orders can deadlock.

trigger: Mail, ship notices or captures run inside a database transaction, or you claim an operation is all or nothing.
body: Send notifications after the commit and log failures, name which operations stay outside the transaction, and inject a failure just after commit to see what state remains. Why: a failing handler inside the money transaction erases the payment, while work after the commit can fail and leave a paid order with an error. Check: a failing mail handler leaves order and payment saved, and the state after a post-commit failure is documented.
evidence: After an order became one transaction a failing notification rolled the payment back; cart emptying after commit could leave a full cart and invite a second identical order; capture at 'Shipped' still ran inside the admin save.

trigger: A new driver or mapper handles typed values (numbers, strings, dates) differently.
body: Write a small tool that scans real or restored data for typed variants of key fields (numbers stored as strings and the reverse) on the old and the new server, and fails on any incompatibility; prove the tool by breaking its input on purpose. Why: a new driver's typed calls throw on values that test fixtures never held. Check: exact counts per type, and a deliberately broken query makes the tool fail instead of passing through a stand-in that ignores its input.
evidence: A census over 203 strings on two server versions; a fake aggregate that ignored its pipeline let a mutation stay green with exit 0 on typed data until the pipeline itself was asserted.

trigger: A singleton authentication provider or service holds per-request state in a field.
body: Do not keep state about one request in a shared object; carry it in a per-request details object, delete the field and setter, and test with barrier-forced interleavings over the real wired beans, including other paths that read the same flag. Why: interleaving logins can leak state from one session into another. Check: race cells are red on the old code and green with the token carrying the flag, and a mutation turns them red again.
evidence: A login flaw that only a concurrency test exposed (2 of 5 race cells were red before the fix).

trigger: After three or more review rounds on the same concurrent mechanism, each round finds a new failure cell.
body: Stop patching after three or more review rounds on one concurrent mechanism that each find a new failure. Write a table of every operation and every way it can fail, state the invariant that must hold at the end whatever fails, and decide in writing what to implement and what to leave as a known limit. Why: the recovery signal was smaller than the state it had to recover, so each fix exposed the next failure. Check: a design note with the table, the root cause in one sentence and the decision.
evidence: A single mechanism took 14 fix rounds and 5 design versions; an end-state invariant (marker state plus retry after any failure) replaced per-mode handling.

trigger: You upgrade Spring Data or a similar layer for a document database.
body: List the indexes on a fresh database created by the old and the new stack and compare definitions including unique flags; recreate them explicitly when automatic creation is off, and make seeds idempotent. Why: unique indexes silently stopped being created and duplicates were accepted. Check: a duplicate insert throws on the new stack and the index lists match collection by collection.
evidence: 17 collections had only the default id index on the new Spring Data stack while the legacy control rejected duplicate accounts; a seed that ran twice then had to be made idempotent.

trigger: Your upgrade was tested only on SQLite or on one database engine, or you make order completion atomic on SQLite.
body: Run the app's own tests and the outside-in suite once on the production database engine, and use IMMEDIATE transactions and lock timeouts on SQLite because select_for_update does nothing there. Why: engines differ on rounding, unsigned columns, strict mode, unknown columns, id reuse after rollback, case sensitivity and locking. Check: per-test outcomes are compared between engines and each difference is treated as a finding.
evidence: On MySQL a money column stored 1501.5 as 1502, a negative total became 0 with no error, a missing column was a 500 only there, and 255 of 278 tests assumed the first id is 1; on SQLite only 2 to 8 of 20 checkouts finished without lock settings.

trigger: A schema or data migration has a down step, or claims old binaries cannot use the upgraded store.
body: Prove a rollback by running forward, reversing, then running the old release on the rows the new code wrote, including a resumed workflow; fence old binaries at every old write path, not one reader. Why: restoring a column does not restore the old meaning of its data, and a version check in one reader leaves other writers open. Check: the old page opens migrated rows or fails cleanly, and every old write entry refuses and leaves rows unchanged.
evidence: Card storage was redesigned from weak reversible encryption to last-4 plus token; the reverse proof found a 500 the forward proof missed; in a data store holding money rows an old binary could still commit money rows after the upgrade until every write path was refused.

trigger: A migration removes or rewrites an encrypted or secret column.
body: After a migration drops or rewrites a column that held a secret, search the storage for the old values. On SQLite turn on secure delete first, then search the database file and its -wal and -journal files. On PostgreSQL run VACUUM FULL and treat WAL archives, backups and replicas as copies that still hold them (this half is advice; it was not tested). Why: dropping or blanking a column leaves the old bytes in free pages and logs. Check: a byte search of the database files, journals, backups and replicas finds none of the old values.
evidence: A payment-credential migration in a ported shop was verified on SQLite only, by searching the database file for the old secret values after the column was dropped; the PostgreSQL steps were not run.

trigger: Tests run only on fresh databases or on data written by the new version, while production holds data written by older releases.
body: Test the upgrade on a populated database written by each previous release (every writer, including optional fields they always filled), and say plainly which old records cannot be classified or what was not tested. Why: new-writer tests miss old shapes, and a fallback to the old algorithm can keep every old bug alive. Check: a regression test loads old-format data and fails on the pre-fix code.
evidence: Nobody tested upgrading a populated database in a Django 2.2 to 3.2 port until one data migration was proven on a real earlier-stage database; a history-keeping data migration left different historical records after removal, rename and forced re-init.

trigger: You compare database state between runs or versions and code reads or updates rows without ORDER BY.
body: Rerun a differing scenario alone on both sides before declaring a version difference, and TRUNCATE tables before each scenario or sort inside the picture. Why: PostgreSQL returns unordered rows in physical order and DELETE leaves dead row versions, so order depends on which tests ran before. Check: a scenario that differed in the full run gives the same result alone.
evidence: A Liberapay lost-chargeback scenario split money into different bundles on two versions (16 cells) yet agreed when run alone; truncating before each story fixed the harness.

trigger: Sessions or signed cookies must stop working after logout or a new login.
body: Bind the signed cookie to a per-login id and require a matching stored record; never recreate a session from a cookie, and rotate the session id on login. Why: a cookie saved before logout stayed valid until it expired, and a session id that stays the same across logins can be reused. Check: probes written as test cells: reuse a saved cookie after logout, reuse the first cookie after a re-login, and two parallel logins.
evidence: In a Java web application port a session outlived logout; a probe written as a test cell showed it, and the first fix still left one path that recreated sessions.

trigger: You record 'confirmed' after publishing to a queue or broker.
body: Find out what the success value means (queue accepted, worker ran, broker acknowledged) and record 'confirmed' only on the signal that proves the effect; allow for thread pools that reorder two quick calls. Why: a publish call returned an id even after it threw, and a pool of five threads reordered two back-to-back publishes. Check: executed probes of the dispatch layer, plus a control with a pool of one that keeps order.
evidence: A publish call returned a non-null id after a swallowed exception, so 'confirmed' would have been false; a retry loop could run about 13 hours.

trigger: A message or job can be delivered more than once (redelivery, retry, double click) and has a side effect.
body: Stop duplicates with a conditional write on the key, or a per-order record written before the side effect; do not rely on a framework's 'run once' or 'no overlap' job feature, which does not deduplicate a redelivered message. Why: those features guard a schedule, not a message, so the second delivery runs the side effect again. Check: deliver the same message twice, and twice at once, and count the side effects, the saved records and the outgoing calls; with the guard removed the count is 2.
evidence: A practice port of an order-handling service onto a key-value store and a message queue, run against local stand-ins (one run).

trigger: A key-value or document store holds decimals (money, quantities) that you read through a vendor SDK.
body: Check how the SDK reads stored decimals: some return floating-point numbers, so large amounts lose precision. Read numbers as strings, or store integer minor units (cents) and convert at the edge. Why: a float cannot hold every large amount exactly, and the error shows only on big or fine values. Check: round-trip a large amount and a fractional amount through save and load on the real SDK version and compare them exactly.
evidence: A practice port of an order-handling service onto a key-value store, run against a local stand-in (one run).

trigger: A worker consumes queue messages and has a side effect before it acknowledges the message.
body: Test a worker killed after the side effect but before it acknowledges the message: the message can be redelivered until it lands in a dead-letter queue, and the order can be lost silently. Probe the saved state and the contents of the dead-letter queue, not only a count of messages. Why: a count can look right while the order exists nowhere. Check: kill the worker at that exact point and show where the order is afterwards: saved, retried, or in the dead-letter queue with its reason.
evidence: A practice port of an order-handling service onto a message queue, run against a local stand-in (one run).

trigger: You replace web.xml and an external servlet container with an executable jar and embedded container.
body: Recover the descriptor contract from version history (servlets, mappings, filters, listeners, missing encoding filter) and reproduce it in code; inventory behaviour that lives outside the code (context parameters, JVM options in start scripts, connector settings) from redacted copies of the real host. Why: auto-configuration adds or drops things silently and ignored settings go live. Check: a request test asserting path and filter order, and a probe that goes red on a planted difference.
evidence: Every route returned a Tomcat 404 because auto-config artifacts were missing; four filter beans ran twice (web.xml had one proxy); the recovered contract had a dispatcher at '/', a version servlet on two paths and no encoding filter.

trigger: The deployed servlet container cannot run the new archive.
body: State plainly that the smoke ran on the target container, not the deployed one; change deployment descriptors by edit-and-diff with an owner checklist per descriptor (OS, init system, service name, bypass paths), and replace unchecked plain-HTTP downloads with HTTPS plus a checksum. Why: the deployed servlet container was too old to host a Jakarta WAR and descriptors carried stale names and OS assumptions. Check: the owner signs off each checklist item.
evidence: Descriptors moved to Tomcat 11 with Temurin 21 and a systemd unit; eleven checklist items; three pre-existing defects found by static read.

trigger: You compare archives between builds.
body: Compare archives by listing contents (library list, file counts, tree fingerprint), not by archive hash, and keep test-scoped and provided jars out. Why: a hash only shows that a file changed (useful to show a new build really differs), not that two builds differ in content: four builds of one tree gave four digests while being identical entry by entry. Check: the library count and names are as expected, test jars are absent and the dist fingerprint matches.
evidence: A security test library and the servlet API were in the archive (62 to 60 and 56 to 55 jars after the scope fix); 4 builds of the same tree gave 4 digests; a 356-file frontend output fingerprint reproduced six times.

trigger: A module in the build reactor builds images or binds external steps, or you run install to test one module.
body: Never run a bare reactor build or install to test one module: exclude modules with docker, native or network steps, use -pl module -am with a per-person local repository, and count project artifacts in shared and home repositories before and after every gate. Why: a default-lifecycle docker build contacted the daemon, and installed artifacts shadow reactor builds. Check: logs show no contact and zero project artifacts in shared caches.
evidence: A messaging module bound a docker build in the default lifecycle; five incidents of installs into shared caches; a smoke recipe had silently depended on a forbidden install; two projects with identical coordinates overwrite each other in a shared repository.

trigger: You route a build tool's cache or temp directory into a project folder while some child processes drop environment variables.
body: Set the cache or temp location in the tool's own global configuration (Maven localRepository, npm cache) and pass explicit properties (-Dmaven.repo.local, -Djava.io.tmpdir); never forward a whole option string through an environment filter, and check the first tool version that reads each variable. Why: variables reach only children whose environment keeps them, and project or user settings can override a global default. Check: build inside the strictest boundary and print where it wrote.
evidence: A Java 8 launcher ignored JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS (read from Java 9 on); a global npm without a project-local pin rewrote a lockfile by 4,190 added and 1,965 removed lines; an environment allowlist kept TEMP and TMP but dropped TMPDIR and cache variables.

trigger: You write a recipe or script that others will run, often on a different platform from yours.
body: A recipe is not done until it has run end to end from a clean checkout on the target platform, twice in a row, from an empty database and cache, with exit status propagated and a scenario with no recorded effect reported as inconclusive rather than failed. Why: your own environment hides holes: line endings, leftover data, shared caches, unpinned drivers, a test job that exited 0 after failed tests. Check: two consecutive clean runs give the same result.
