evidence: A recipe tested on Windows failed on Linux in four ways (CRLF in a shell script, a second run on the same database, a shared cache folder, an unpinned driver); a clean-checkout run of another recipe found six holes; a suite job exited 0 after failed tests.

trigger: You build an app image with a shared dockerignore file, or claim the tested image is the built image.
body: Compare the built image's file tree with a manifest of the commit, bind the running container to its immutable image id and config (User, Env, StopSignal, entrypoint), and anchor ignore patterns to the folder you mean (/vendor, not **/vendor). Why: an ignore rule silently dropped the app's own nested vendor folders, and equal layers can carry a different user or stop signal. Check: the tree equals the manifest, and a wrong image or a one-byte change fails the gate.
evidence: The **/vendor pattern dropped 49 of Crater's own files (mail templates, backup translations) and suites still passed; after the rebuild 1,415 of 1,415 files (new) and 1,397 of 1,397 (old) matched.

trigger: You build a base image for Kubernetes with a non-root user, a read-only root or mounted config files.
body: End the image with a numeric USER (such as 33 or 10001), copy config files in rather than bind-mounting into a sticky world-writable web root, and for a read-only root list every write location (temp, thumbnails, caches, control sockets, installer files) with its own writable volume. Why: the kubelet refuses a named user under runAsNonRoot, and fs.protected_regular blocks writes to bind-mounted files. Check: start the container as it will run, with the installer and the first request.
evidence: Both a PHP and a Python image named their user and were refused by the kubelet; a bind-mounted .env made the installer fail to save; a Python app needed a temp dir, a thumbnail folder and the web server's control socket moved.

trigger: You move a PHP app into php-fpm or behind an egress proxy and pass configuration or secrets through the environment.
body: php-fpm clears the environment by default, so set clear_env to no for secrets and settings. Guzzle ignores the upper-case HTTP_PROXY variable outside the command line (use lower-case http_proxy), while HTTPS_PROXY is read everywhere; better still, enforce no-egress with a network that has no route out. Why: the container held the secret but the app answered 500, and a proxy meant to watch outgoing calls was bypassed for plain http. Check: log in with the secret's database password and see a deliberate outside call reach the tripwire.
evidence: With php-fpm defaults the app answered 500 'No application encryption key' and tried MySQL on 127.0.0.1; with two Guzzle 7 releases plain http bypassed the tripwire while https was carried by every mechanism.

trigger: A Deployment with a migration Job, a readiness probe and more than one replica.
body: Run installs and migrations in a separate Job, make readiness depend on the complete schema (applied migrations equal the files in the image plus a marker written after seeding), label web and job pods differently so the Service selects web pods only, and keep job reruns idempotent. Why: a home-page or row-count probe passes on a half-migrated schema and the Job pod became a ready endpoint. Check: pause the Job halfway and log EndpointSlices; no pod is ready.
evidence: A probe on '/' let pods report ready before the Job finished and 49 of 49 suite runs failed; a row-count probe passed at 63 of 126 migrations; a Job pod was a ready endpoint for 55 s; a second Job run failed seeding on a duplicate admin.

trigger: You roll a Deployment under traffic, or explain a restart or shutdown failure by 'SIGTERM'.
body: Add a preStop delay (a few seconds) so the pod leaves the Service before it stops, set resource requests as well as limits so the surge pod can schedule, give tests a warm-up for fresh pods, and read the image's real StopSignal before explaining a failure; change one factor at a time. Why: requests fail during rolling restarts and the assumed SIGTERM story was wrong. Check: a load test across a rolling restart with and without the hook.
evidence: Without a hook 21 requests failed (15 in the restart minute), with sleep 10 alone 0; in a second app 5 of 18 suite runs failed without preStop and 0 of 20 with it; both images stopped with SIGQUIT; a load test lost the first 6 requests of fresh pods.

trigger: You claim a Kubernetes NetworkPolicy or an internal network cuts the test environment off from the outside.
body: Prove the cut-off from inside the pod with a control: the same probe from a policy-free pod must reach a stand-in host and the app pod must not; check the union of all egress rules that select the app pods and probe every serving pod; block the host and its ports too. Why: policy can be silently unenforced and an internal network only keeps out the internet. Check: the gate refuses an extra rule, a missing probe and a down control.
evidence: k3s started with --node-ip silently enforced no policy (0 per-pod chains); an internal Docker network kept the internet out but a pod reached the VM's port 22; a gate passed an extra egress rule it never probed; a k3s run listed seven things it could not show.

trigger: You move to containers and a new language version together.
body: Run the same code on the current language version in the container first, and keep a two-by-two table (host or container, current or new version). Why: in three Python projects whose earlier runs were on Windows, more results changed with the move to Linux than with the new language version. Check: the table attributes each change to one factor.
evidence: On 3 Python projects, Linux containers removed 8 of 9 and 3 of 3 Windows failures, while Python 3.14 changed nothing in two and blocked one at import.

trigger: You prepare an upgrade of a service whose ports and data are live, or reuse the previous upgrade's scripts.
body: Rehearse on a copy of the data built by the old runtime, run the new version's pre-start checks one by one, hand the same data back to the old runtime to prove rollback, make rollback recover partial writes from a verified original without depending on the failed runtime, and start the next window from the fixed scripts of the last. Why: reverse string replacement does not recover a partial write. Check: the log shows each check, one real transaction and an old-runtime read of new data.
evidence: A service switch's window check failed at step one because the package was built from an unfixed older script that expected a pre-migration value; operator upgrade reviews found partially rewritten configs and rollback checkers that picked a broken new runtime.

trigger: Before declaring a slice or an evidence pack done.
body: Have a reader who has not seen the plan or expectations read the diff against the baseline commit, with neutral wording and no hint of the conclusion; give the evidence pack to someone who did not follow the work. Why: cold readers find classes of defects that briefed reviewers miss. Check: the brief states only the commit range and baseline, and findings come back severity-tagged.
evidence: A cold read at one Java slice found read-side defaults, a stale database process, a test double skipped on every gate and a hard-coded guard; a cold read of an evidence pack found 8 serious, 12 medium and 10 small corrections.

trigger: A team is about to declare a port or upgrade done on its own evidence (self-certified).
body: Give the finished, committed work to an independent reader, ideally built by a different vendor or tool, who rebuilds it from the written recipe in a clean checkout and tries to break it. Why: the team's tests and same-vendor reviewers share its blind spots. Check: the reader reproduces every test id and outcome from a clean checkout and returns a verdict with severity-tagged findings.
evidence: In a 2012 shop port the outside reader gave NO-GO on a port tagged faithful and found 3 regressions, a suite gap and a false claim; on a PHP upgrade it found 3 more faults the suite missed (mail encryption ignored, backups unlistable, a client-address spoof).

trigger: You review a long series of small porting commits, or a review confirms one finding.
body: Besides per-commit verdicts, sweep the whole slice for each known class of porting fault (removed APIs on every path, ordering, bytes versus text, shared state, equal sort keys), and treat one confirmed finding as an instance of a class. Why: per-commit review leans on the suite and never asks where else the same mistake lives. Check: each class has a recorded search and result.
evidence: A port with 24 per-commit verdicts (7 rejections) still reached the tag with 3 error-path regressions and a false thread-safety claim; a class sweep then found 7 more, including a 500 on every configurable product page and a zip-slip write.

trigger: Old and new behaviour differ, you decide to accept the new one, and a golden file must be re-recorded.
body: Record the old contract, the new behaviour, the layer where it happens, the decision and the owner, and re-pin the fixture with a diff review, never a blind re-record. Why: silent re-recording destroys the baseline. Check: the golden diff is empty unless a declared re-record has a recorded review.
evidence: A router-level 404 became a firewall 400, a logout response gained a cookie-clearing header that was a mock artefact, and one search route stayed broken in production both before and after.

trigger: Findings need a decision from the system's owner, a defect turns out to be a business rule, or the migration surfaces bugs older than itself.
body: Keep a decision document for the owner with release-blocking, scope and information items; write business-rule oddities and old bugs down as questions with the code or commit showing current intent, classify each as migration-caused, pre-existing or unknown, and do not change them silently. Why: maintainers may have meant it, and fixing one cause of a coupled symptom closes neither. Check: each item has an owner, a question and what it blocks.
evidence: Six release-blocking and seven scope decisions were recorded for a Java programme; refund-cap and frozen-basket-price rules were left as owner questions; defects older than the migration (unbounded recursion in a scheduling routine, a substring taken from a too-short identifier) were registered, not silently fixed.

trigger: Improvement ideas appear while you migrate.
body: Define the finish line as same behaviour on the new stack, proven, park UI rewrites, refactors and new features until after acceptance, and have the owner ratify an out-of-scope list; faults already in the old code go to the owner as decisions, not into the migration. Why: improvement slices consumed many review rounds and diluted the migration. Check: a written finish line and an out-of-scope list the owner has signed.
evidence: A React UI and code-improvement slices were wound down at the owner's request after about a week; acceptance used the original dataset and a screen walk only.

trigger: You write a result page, release note or summary for a migration.
body: Write every claim at the size of its proof and name the boundary of each all-or-nothing or once claim; search the code before writing that something is not done; do not write 'all differences come from the framework' unless the probe fed inputs that would show an app-level difference. Why: reviewers repeatedly found sentences stronger than the code. Check: each claim pairs with a test, command or probe and states its boundary.
evidence: A page claimed order completion was all or nothing though the cart was emptied after commit, and that a rejected ZIP changes nothing though a staging file could delete an existing one; 4 of 6 blind runs over-claimed 'same except framework differences' with three cases unprobed; a guide said hung tools are not detected while a default-on watchdog existed.

trigger: A result page cites test counts, lint numbers or artifact files.
body: Regenerate every number and file at the final commit, read counts out of the committed result files and compare them with the page, name the exact commit beside each artifact, and keep a clean run's worktree until its files are committed. Why: a page's final count was backed by an older run that still held a withdrawn test. Check: counts parsed from the tagged files equal the page, and a fresh run on the tag matches.
evidence: A result page's test count (1,446) came from an older run containing a withdrawn test; a lint table quoted 462 and 56 findings from the stage tip while the tag measured 466 and 55; the close review rejected it.

trigger: You write the result of a migration or claim a change is safe on several platforms.
body: End with a 'not run' list and a 'which runs count' note: name the platforms, databases and scenarios actually executed (read the CI matrix), label one run per variant as one run, and say what a single-node or laptop environment cannot show. Why: it makes the size of the proof visible and honest. Check: every claim matches an entry in proved or not run.
evidence: Both blind migration runs had long not-proven lists, the best sign of calibration; a probe page listed 9 items not run (arm64, Kubernetes, a second run of each suite); a cross-platform claim rested on one runner.

trigger: You hand over a newcomer's guide to a system you just ported.
body: Test the guide blind: questions and an answer key written from the code by someone who has not read the guide, a fresh reader answering from the guide alone, and a control from the project's own docs; write the business rules and what really happens on the default path, not only code layout. Why: the author's own questions give a flattering score. Check: graded scores per category and a list of material errors with file and line.
evidence: A guide scored 10/10 on the author's questions, 6.5/10 on the reviewer's and 1.5/5 on business rules, then 8.5/12 with a rules section; for another project it scored 9.0 of 12 against the project's own docs at 3.0 of 12.

trigger: You write or review a setup guide, runbook or replay recipe that tells a reader to run commands.
body: Run every step exactly as written in a throwaway environment of the exact release, as a newcomer would, and record which commands were run and which were not, with prerequisites, clean-up between steps and the real output line. Why: reading alone missed install sources, hidden items and a failing step that cost 13 minutes. Check: someone who did not write it reproduces the stated output.
evidence: A throwaway run of a setup guide found six issues invisible from reading; a replay quoted from a script header stopped for lack of an interpreter path and, once fixed, ran 13 minutes before failing on a missing environment while the real check took 18 seconds.

trigger: A migration run ends and its evidence lives in a side folder.
body: Leave a guard test in the repository for each fixed trap, and keep the output of each removal proof, not just a claim. Also keep four records of a well-run migration: the frozen list of test ids from the old version, a dump of the silent defaults, removal proofs that show the restored code identical to the original, and repeat runs from clean copies. Why: evidence in a side folder guards nothing for the next maintainer. Check: reverting each trap fix in a copy turns a repository test red.
evidence: In one blind run all 5 reverts were caught by 11 added in-repo tests; in another 0 of 5 because no tests were added; in a second round only 3 of 6 runs left any in-repo guard and 1 kept removal output; the best run (5.5 of 6) kept all four artefacts.
